title: Why Confidence Shrinks When Dealing With Senior Leaders
author: Admired Leadership
summary: An account of a specific failure of professional presence: leaders who are assured with their own teams becoming deferential, passive and obsequious in front of high-status clients or senior colleagues. The behavioural markers are catalogued precisely — deferring more, speaking less, agreeing quickly, adding disclaimers, excessive politeness — and the cost is framed as lost credibility and lost influence rather than mere awkwardness. The explanation offered separates healthy adaptation from pathology: all effective leaders adjust to context, but a subset are so status-attuned that they are continuously ranking the room, which produces boldness downward and collapse upward. Because the same trait drives both behaviours, the person’s subordinates would scarcely recognise them in a senior meeting. The coaching prescription is to abandon attention to hierarchy and anchor on substance and content, resisting the urge to seek approval, with the reminder that high-status people are just people.
points: The tell is asymmetry: the same leader acts powerfully around those they rank below them and passively around those they rank above, which points to status-attunement rather than to timidity.

The author catalogues the specific behaviours that erode credibility — quick agreement, disclaimers, reduced speech and excessive politeness — making the problem observable rather than a vague impression.
A useful distinction is drawn between normal situational adaptation, which effective leaders do, and the extreme version that makes a person unrecognisable to their own reports.
The recommended coaching intervention is to redirect attention from people to issues — focus exclusively on substance and content — rather than to exhort the person to be more confident.
quotes: Otherwise formidable and self-confident leaders can sometimes turn into shape-shifting lizards in the presence of powerful and high-status colleagues or clients.
They come across as reticent, junior, passive, and obsequious. The weak style they project erodes their credibility and reduces their influence.
They defer more, speak less, agree quickly, offer disclaimers, and become overly polite.
Because they want to be accepted and liked by those with more influence, they modify their behavior to achieve that objective.
Their heightened focus on their own status influences them to act powerfully and boldly when surrounded by those they view as having less status.
If you know a leader who adapts too much around high-status people, the best advice is to ask them to shed their concern for status and to focus exclusively on substance and content.
Reminding them that status shouldn’t define who they are can sometimes help as well.
